papers.title: Dynamical Batching: How Class-Cycling Training Shapes the Internal Structure of Neural Networks
papers.abstract: We investigate whether cyclically varying the class composition of training batches can modify both the performance and the internal organization of neural networks. Motivated by nonequilibrium systems, in which cycling between related sub-goals can make switching between their solutions increasingly efficient, we introduce Dynamical Batching (DB), a sampling protocol that periodically emphasizes each class while leaving the loss and the optimizer unchanged, and compare it with Uniform Batching (UB), in which every mini-batch has equal class proportions. In the regime where standard training fails, DB changes the outcome: on a three-arm spiral, a capacity-limited MLP that plateaus far below perfect accuracy under UB fits the training data under DB. Tracking individual weights, we find that under DB the change between class-specialized states is carried by a smaller set of weights than under UB, and that this set is markedly more persistent from cycle to cycle, on every synthetic dataset we test and in a wider network that fits the data under both protocols. This organization is a signature of the protocol rather than a predictor of its benefit: it appears equally where DB leaves accuracy unchanged. On CIFAR-10, the same protocol modestly improves the test accuracy of a channel-narrowed ResNet-10, a standard residual architecture, and of a second capacity-limited convolutional network. These results show that how class emphasis is distributed in time can shape both the solution a network reaches and the internal structure of the network.

papers.title: Undulatory Swimming in Sand: Subsurface Locomotion of the Sandfish Lizard
papers.abstract: The desert-dwelling sandfish (Scincus scincus) moves within dry sand, a material that displays solid and fluidlike behavior. High-speed x-ray imaging shows that below the surface, the lizard no longer uses limbs for propulsion but generates thrust to overcome drag by propagating an undulatory traveling wave down the body. Although viscous hydrodynamics can predict swimming speed in fluids such as water, an equivalent theory for granular drag is not available. To predict sandfish swimming speed, we developed an empirical model by measuring granular drag force on a small cylinder oriented at different angles relative to the displacement direction and summing these forces over the animal movement profile. The agreement between model and experiment implies that the noninertial swimming occurs in a frictional fluid.

papers.title: Quantifying the Kinetic and Thermodynamic Origins of the Glass-Forming Ability in Metals
papers.abstract: The glass-forming ability (GFA) of a metallic liquid can be quantified by the critical cooling rate $R_c$, below which it crystallizes upon cooling. $R_c$ is determined by the competition between $R$ and the crystallization rate $\mathcal{K}_{\rm X}$. Here, we calculate $R_c$ and $\mathcal{K}_{\rm X}$ in model pure metals and alloys with BCC/B2 and FCC equilibrium crystal structures. Using classical nucleation theory and independently calculated crystal growth rates, we evaluate $\mathcal{K}_{\rm X}=(IU^3)^{1/4}$ at $T=0.8T_m$, where $I$ and $U$ are the nucleation and growth rates and $T_m$ is the melting temperature. We find a strong positive correlation between $\mathcal{K}_{\rm X}$ and $R_c$ over eleven orders of magnitude. We decompose $\mathcal{K}_{\rm X}$ into a product of a kinetic contribution, involving atomic cluster attachment and diffusion, and a thermodynamic contribution. We show that the thermodynamic contribution to $\mathcal{K}_{\rm X}$ dominates the kinetic contribution over the range of cooling rates that we consider. The nucleation barrier $\Delta G_c \sim \tilde\gamma^3/\Delta\tilde\mu^2$, where $\tilde\gamma$ is the reduced effective liquid--crystal interfacial free energy and $\Delta\tilde\mu$ is the reduced bulk driving force, determines the magnitude of the thermodynamic contribution. The relative importance of $\tilde\gamma$ and $\Delta\tilde\mu$ depends on the material: a large interfacial free energy can suppress nucleation in some systems, whereas a weak bulk driving force can inhibit crystallization in others. Analyses of the structural and chemical order show that better glass formers have enhanced structural frustration, more icosahedral-like and less crystal-like local environments, and a larger chemical-order mismatch between the supercooled liquid and crystal phases.

papers.title: Mode coupling theory analysis of water dynamics detected by dielectric spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Mode-coupling theory (MCT), one of the most prominent models of the glass transition, also makes various specific predictions for the molecular dynamics in the liquid state of matter. They can be best experimentally tested by evaluating susceptibility spectra covering a broad frequency range. In the present work, we clarify whether the most recent broadband dielectric-spectroscopy results on water, whose glass transition is highly disputed, are compatible with MCT. The so-called fast beta process, expected within this theory, should be detectable at low temperatures only, inaccessible in water due to its inevitable crystallization upon cooling. Therefore, we also investigate data on aqueous LiCl solutions, which can be easily supercooled. We find that all the available broadband dielectric data on these solutions and pure water are well consistent with MCT. Notably, this includes the expected interrelation of the critical temperature dependence of the alpha relaxation to its often-neglected non-Debye spectral shape. Moreover, the available data on the fast beta process, detected in a 14.8 mol% LiCl solution, are also well consistent with the theory. We find a smooth development of the derived MCT parameters with salt concentration which supports the validity of the critical temperature Tc = 222 K and system parameter lambda = 0.55 deduced here for pure water. We also compare the current dielectric relaxation-time results to those determined by other experimental methods and address the question whether information on the controversial fragile-to-strong transition of water can be obtained from such data. Finally, we discuss the significance of the dominant dielectric relaxation process of water for the glass transition as described by MCT, especially considering scenarios questioning its association with the alpha relaxation.

papers.title: Dependence of the acoustic propulsion of nano- and microcones on their orientation and aspect ratio
papers.abstract: Recent research revealed the orientation-dependent propulsion of a cone-shaped colloidal particle that is exposed to a planar traveling ultrasound wave. Here, we extend the previous research by considering nano- and microcones with different aspect ratios and studying how the propulsion of a particle depends on its orientation and aspect ratio. We also study how the orientation-averaged propulsion of a cone-shaped particle, which corresponds to an isotropic ultrasound field, depends on its aspect ratio and identify an aspect ratio of 1/2 where the orientation-averaged propulsion is particularly strong. To make our simulation results easier reusable for follow-up research, we provide a corresponding simple analytic representation.

papers.title: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media
papers.abstract: Legged locomotion on flowing ground ({\em e.g.} granular media) is unlike locomotion on hard ground because feet experience both solid- and fluid-like forces during surface penetration. Recent bio-inspired legged robots display speed relative to body size on hard ground comparable to high performing organisms like cockroaches but suffer significant performance loss on flowing materials like sand. In laboratory experiments we study the performance (speed) of a small (2.3 kg) six-legged robot, SandBot, as it runs on a bed of granular media (1 mm poppy seeds). For an alternating tripod gait on the granular bed, standard gait control parameters achieve speeds at best two orders of magnitude smaller than the 2 body lengths/s ($\approx 60$ cm/s) for motion on hard ground. However, empirical adjustment of these control parameters away from the hard ground settings, restores good performance, yielding top speeds of 30 cm/s. Robot speed depends sensitively on the packing fraction $\phi$ and the limb frequency $\omega$, and a dramatic transition from rotary walking to slow swimming occurs when $\phi$ becomes small enough and/or $\omega$ large enough. We propose a kinematic model of the rotary walking mode based on generic features of penetration and slip of a curved limb in granular media. The model captures the dependence of robot speed on limb frequency and the transition between walking and swimming modes but highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the physics of granular media.

papers.title: Unambiguous characterization of in-plane dielectric response in nanoconfined liquids: water as a case study
papers.abstract: The in-plane dielectric constant of nanoconfined water has attracted growing interest in recent years. Nevertheless, assigning a bulk-like dielectric constant to a molecularly thin film is convention dependent because it requires choosing an effective water width. We propose the in-plane 2D polarizability, $\alpha_{\parallel}$, as a macroscopic characterization of the in-plane dielectric response that avoids this choice. Using classical molecular dynamics simulations, we compute $\alpha_{\parallel}$ via two independent and consistent methods: based on fluctuation-dissipation theory, and from the induced dipole moment when water is placed in a capacitor. Our results provide the framework to quantify the in-plane dielectric response of polar liquids across simulations and experiments.

papers.title: Microphase Separation and Ionic Aggregation in Oppositely Charged End-Functionalized Polymer Blends
papers.abstract: We study the phase behavior of binary blends of polymers with oppositely charged termini using an ion-correlation-augmented self-consistent field theory (IC-SCFT). Under the low dielectric conditions typical for organic polymer melts, strong ion correlations drive association of multiple chain ends, leading to emergent multichain architectures that go beyond a simple ion-paired diblock copolymer picture previously used to interpret recent experiments. At moderate to strong polymer segregation, the resulting phase diagram differs considerably from this effective-diblock prediction: ion clustering broadens the lamellar and cylindrical windows while suppressing the network phases, the reverse of the trend for end-charged diblock copolymers. At weak segregation, the two polymers remain miscible even as ion clustering persists, and decreasing chain length drives the clusters themselves through a sphere-to-cylinder-to-lamella shape transition, connecting continuously to the aggregation behavior of classical terminally charged ionomers in the limit when one of the polymer species shrinks to just the charged end. These results reveal that ion clustering -- beyond simple pairwise bonding -- shapes the self-assembly of end-charged polymer blends.

papers.title: Calibrated shape-only recovery of membrane viscosities
papers.abstract: Nearby relaxation rates make two membrane viscosities difficult to distinguish from a shape transient. We show how calibrated preparation removes this loss of local sensitivity in a linear Kelvin-Voigt sphere with finite area elasticity and intrinsic membrane dissipation. Two independent releases, with a known signed amplitude ratio and calibrated relative gain and timing, yield normal-displacement records whose fixed linear combination separates the shear and dilatational rates. Their common amplitude remains unknown. For fixed sampling, positive-definite weights, bounded positive rates and nonzero excitation, the amplitude-projected sensitivity has a positive lower bound even at rate coincidence. Without relative calibration, the paired sensitivity decreases linearly with the rate gap; the single tangential-release record decreases quadratically. The calibrated bound is compatible with fixed finite initial energy. A positive local bound also persists with independent ratio calibration of fixed positive precision under a Gaussian error model. Supplied elastic coefficients convert the recovered rates into the two surface viscosities. An unbounded spherical Stokes extension quantifies how bulk dissipation changes the modal patterns and provides a sufficient full-Jacobian criterion for retaining local material sensitivity.

papers.title: Three-body corrections to Brownian hard-sphere viscosity
papers.abstract: For Brownian hard spheres without hydrodynamic interactions, we obtain a conditional enclosure between 1.8266948 and 1.8267157 for the third-order zero-shear Brownian viscosity coefficient. It applies when the physical three-body correction coincides with the finite-energy weak solution and the remote remainder in the pair adjoint identity vanishes. Kirkwood superposition gives zero because three nonzero pair contributions cancel exactly. An elementary radial identity exposes this cancellation, and a common contact-stress convention allows direct comparison of closure predictions. Although superposition solves the bulk equation, it leaves a shared-contact flux error. Correcting this error defines a unique weak response with positive Dirichlet energy. Explicit symmetric trials yield a variational lower bound and a residual upper bound using the rotational structure of shear and three-sphere geometry. Exact integration and outward interval evaluation enclose the fixed-trial functionals. Under the stated physical conditions, the resulting interval excludes all closure coefficients compared here and supplies a quantitative benchmark for dilute three-body Brownian stress.

papers.title: Active rheology shapes collective flows in uniaxially compressed 3D spheroids
papers.abstract: How compression changes both the magnitude and organization of cell motion remains unclear. Using a three-dimensional active vertex model, we examine how tissue state and active dynamics shape the response of confined spheroids to uniaxial compression. With polarity alignment switched off, compression enhances transverse motion in solid-like spheroids throughout the tested activity range, whereas the fluid-like response reverses from acceleration at low activity to slowing at high activity. Changes in contact persistence organize these responses along a common empirical trend. Passive five-cell calculations reveal how compression reshapes local rearrangement barriers: the response depends on geometry and loading direction, and a high-strain increase in the fluid-like mean coexists with many low-barrier paths. In a separate high-alignment regime, strong compression induces coherent rotation in solid-like spheroids, while fluid-like spheroids show no comparable collective rotation. The rotating solids have a higher contact-persistence index than the fluids and exhibit tangential peripheral cell organization. Controlled perturbations reveal compression-induced softening of a differential-twist mode and slower relaxation with activity. Together, these results identify an activity-dependent reversal of the motility response and compression-induced coherent rotation as two distinct outcomes of loading, linking them to contact persistence, local rearrangement costs, and active coordination.

papers.title: Run-and-tumble particles in a harmonic external field: constructing the solution of the Fokker-Planck equation from the equations of motion
papers.abstract: A method for integrating the Langevin equations of motion for run-and-tumble particles is introduced to compute the joint distribution of their position and active velocity, with and without a harmonic external force field. The key step is the construction of the moments of the distribution and the correlation functions, conditional on the particles being in a specific state at the final time. For one-dimensional run-and-tumble particles in a harmonic external potential, the exact steady-state distributions for the tumble state, as well as for the run state conditional on a specified velocity direction, are obtained. This enables us to demonstrate their equivalence to the exact solutions of the corresponding Fokker-Planck equations.

papers.title: Enhancement of liquid-liquid phase transition under shear flow
papers.abstract: In a liquid--liquid transition (LLT), a single-component liquid transforms into another liquid with different density and viscosity. Flow therefore couples to the transition, but the effect of shear flow is not understood. Here we investigate the LLT under shear with a two-order-parameter hydrodynamic model in which the viscosity depends on the non-conserved structural order parameter. Under shear, a fluctuation of the order parameter drives a compressional flow through the viscosity, and the resulting density change enhances the order parameter fluctuation. In a linear analysis, this feedback destabilizes the metastable liquid above a critical shear rate $\dot{\gamma}_{\rm c}$ for wavevectors in particular directions. Because the flow rotates the wavevector, a fluctuation grows only for a finite time duration, and its amplification is determined by the dimensionless shear rate $\dot{\gamma}/\dot{\gamma}_{\rm c}$ and the second dimensionless number $\Lambda$, the ratio of the thermodynamic relaxation rate of the order parameter to $\dot{\gamma}_{\rm c}$. In hydrodynamic simulations, shear above about $\dot{\gamma}_{\rm c}$ induces the transition in the metastable region when $\Lambda\gtrsim1$. The transition proceeds by nucleation of domains whose morphology becomes anisotropic. The incubation time decreases and the onset of the viscosity increase is accelerated as $\dot{\gamma}$ and $\Lambda$ increase. These results imply that the shear rate is a control variable of LLT in addition to temperature and pressure, selecting whether and how a metastable liquid transforms.

papers.title: Emergent Chirality Reversal in Magnetically Driven Rotor Clusters
papers.abstract: Does a collection of magnetically driven rotors necessarily rotate in the same direction as its individual members? We show that rotors driven by a rotating magnetic field self-assemble into clusters whose collective rotation can oppose the self-rotation of every rotor within them. The reversal arises from competition between rotation-translation coupling and dipolar interactions, which favor opposite directions of collective rotation. Their balance varies with system size and driving frequency, producing a transition between the two handed states, while hydrodynamic interactions shift the transition boundary. Collective handedness can thus emerge opposite to the field-imposed single-rotor rotation without reversing the external field, and can be tuned through system size and driving frequency.

papers.title: Flaw-tolerant recycling of waste tires into high-performance rubber
papers.abstract: Annually about one billion tires reach the end of life. Rubber from waste tires can be ground into particles and incorporated into a matrix. In practice, the resulting composites are commonly not recycled into new tires, but downcycled into low-value products such as sport surfaces, indoor flooring, and rubberized asphalt. Recycling waste tires into new tires remains a challenge. In particular, such composites typically have low strength, especially when the particle content is high or the particles are large. A single waste tire particle may act as a flaw to initiate macroscopic fracture and knock down the strength of the entire composite. Here we propose the principle of flaw-tolerant recycling. Rather than requiring every particle to be reliable and small, the matrix is designed so that flaw-like particles do not initiate macroscopic fracture. We demonstrate a flaw-tolerant matrix consisting of two intertwined networks: a network of densely entangled and sparsely crosslinked long natural rubber chains, and a percolated network of carbon aggregates. When the flaw-tolerant matrix is incorporated with up to 80 wt% of commercially available waste particles, the resulting composites still maintain strength. The principle of flaw-tolerant recycling may aid the development of recycling waste tires into new tires.

papers.title: Effect of chirality on active elastomers and solids in three dimensions
papers.abstract: We examine the effect of chiral activity on nematic and polar uniaxial elastomers and solids by constructing the general hydrodynamic equations for these phases. We start with the elastomer, which is not only invariant under rigid rotations but also under an independent rotation of the uniaxial direction, and show that this higher symmetry strongly constrains the effects of chiral activity. We then break the elastomeric symmetry by adding a symmetry-breaking term to the free energy but still retain invariance under rigid rotations. The resulting state has the symmetry of a uniaxial solid, and we show that in a fixed background medium chiral activity generically destabilises it. The force density responsible for this {{instability}} vanishes as the field that breaks the elastomeric symmetry goes to zero. Further, the presence of the symmetry-breaking field also allows for an additional odd elastic force density that generically destabilises momentum-conserved chiral and uniaxial solids in the inertial regime.

papers.title: Chirality destroys oriented active solids
papers.abstract: We construct a hydrodynamic theory of the effect of chiral and active force densities on three-dimensional uniaxial solids. We show that in a fixed background medium active chiral force densities---that arise at lower order in gradients than odd elasticity---generically destabilise the solid state. We further show this active instability also affects isotropic chiral solids in an anisotropic medium, a situation that is relevant for cell clusters moving through the extracellular matrix. Interestingly, the instability is eliminated in a higher-symmetry solid, known as the polar elastomer; indeed, we show that chirality does not affect the leading-order mechanics of such materials. We further demonstrate that momentum-conserving polar active solids have two chiral odd elasticities in contrast to the one discussed for two-dimensional solids. However, we again find that the higher symmetry of polar elastomers eliminates one of these with the remaining one being equivalent to the two-dimensional odd elastic force density. Our results should apply to numerous biological and condensed matter systems.

papers.title: evaluating local viscoelastic properties of artery-mimicking phantoms using high-resolution flexural wavenumber analysis
papers.abstract: The measurement of guided wave propagation is an effective approach for evaluating arterial wall stiffness. A more comprehensive characterization of viscoelastic material properties could yield more informative biomarkers; however, this additionally requires estimation of wave attenuation. Furthermore, spatially local estimation is necessary for localized pathologies, such as atherosclerotic plaques. To this end, we propose an original two-stage high-resolution method to recover local viscoelastic properties from guided waves in artery-like soft tubes. First, the local frequency-wavenumber dispersion relation including losses is estimated using a high-resolution complex wavenumber identification method. Second, assuming a fractional Kelvin-Voigt rheological model for the tube wall, we estimate the viscoelastic material parameters by fitting the dispersion relation computed with a spectral element method to this estimate. We experimentally validate the proposed approach on flexural wave propagation along water-filled soft tubes, measured with a high-speed camera coupled with digital image correlation. Owing to the high resolution of the method, the axial modulus variation of a graded phantom is recovered. Finally, a Cram\'er-Rao analysis indicates that the complex wavenumber estimator operates near its theoretical limit, and reveals why local attenuation is intrinsically difficult to recover.

papers.title: Twitching fiberboids in the collective : A table-top, one-dimensional, active particle gas
papers.abstract: Fiberboids are filaments that self-propel by rolling along a surface due to a flux normal to that surface. In the last few years, fibers using several materials and driving mechanisms have been developed that are able to roll persistently. Here we show using thermally driven nylon fibers on a slightly curved glass surface, that fiberboids also come in another state, that we call ``twitching'': the fiber rolls for a short time and then switches direction, implementing on large scales a diffusion-like motion. We rationalize the occurrence of this effect and experimentally quantify this new dynamic state. We then analyze ensembles of twitching fiberboids and by confining the fibers inside a circular arena to allow them to roll on a single axis only, we implement a simple, table-top realization of a one-dimensional non-equilibrium active gas. We study experimentally active cluster formation, their non-equilibrium dynamics and we rationalize the observations by a simple lattice model. This model takes into account a Viscek-like alignment of the velocity directions of the individual particles within clusters to yield good qualitative agreement with the experiments. Overall our work opens the path to study collectives of self-rolling fibers as an interesting new class of active matter.

papers.title: Superstability of micrometer viscous jets surrounded by weakly-elastic viscous shells
papers.abstract: Our experiments demonstrate the strong stabilizing effect of a viscoelastic shell on flow-focused viscous jets. The results suggest that stabilization occurs when the polymer viscosity, $\eta_p$, exceeds a critical threshold, provided the extensional relaxation time, $\lambda$, is large enough to allow the polymer molecules to undergo the coil-stretch transition. Under these conditions, substantial extensional viscoelastic stresses develop as the liquid accelerates. Since both $\eta_p$ and $\lambda$ increase with shell viscosity, the polymer concentration required to stabilize the viscous jet decreases accordingly. Remarkably, moderately to highly viscous jets can be stabilized with very small polymer concentrations, for which no beads-on-a-string (BOAS) instability is observed.

papers.title: Tunable annealing of defects in self-aligning active crystals
papers.abstract: Obtaining defect-free single-crystals is of crucial importance in soft matter and materials science, spanning both fundamental interests and practical applications. Active crystals, encompassing diverse dense systems from living organisms to artificial metamaterials, can offer a promising platform for autonomous structural reorganization. We demonstrate that increasing spatiotemporal orientational fluctuations around the mean polarized state can enhance crystallographic order in active crystals. Poly-to-single-crystal transformations in defect-rich, self-aligned active Brownian crystals with coupled translational-rotational dynamics are investigated. We show that long-lived persistence with slow alignment controls the defect-annealing capability. By disentangling activity magnitude from associated timescales, we reveal activity-assisted annealing. Tuning the persistence length enables overcoming thermal energy barriers. Simultaneously adjusting persistence and alignment timescales can tune relaxation from `fast' to `slow', yielding defect-rich and defect-free crystals, respectively. Furthermore, active crystals of point particles are found to exhibit similar defect annealing when flocking is delayed by tuning the timescale of the velocity relaxation towards the polarized state. These findings suggest that the mechanism may extend to a broader class of active crystals. Our results intersect statistical physics of living soft matter with the mechanics of defects and microstructures, proposing a nonequilibrium route towards reconfigurable materials.

papers.title: Modular Landau Analysis of Coupled Phase Transitions: Application to Ferroelectric Liquid Crystals
papers.abstract: In systems with coupled order parameters, the relaxation of existing order can modify subsequent transitions, while cooperation and competition between emerging modes can produce complex phase sequences. We develop a modular Landau analysis that locally relaxes noncritical parent-phase variables to obtain effective one- and two-mode free energies. The resulting coefficients quantify relaxation-induced changes in transition characteristics and mode coupling, including changes in transition order for even-symmetry modes. The resulting modules are assembled successively along parent branches, and the equilibrium phase sequence is selected by comparing the fully relaxed free energies of the admissible branches. We apply the framework to ferroelectric liquid crystals, where orientational, polar, smectic, and tilt orders interact and give rise to multiple competing pathways, using a uniaxial model with longitudinal polarization. We fit the model to the measurements reported by Strachan et al. [Adv. Sci. 12(3), 2409754 (2025)]. A single thermodynamic parameter set reproduces the observed transition temperatures, transition types, and phase sequence, while capturing the main birefringence trend. Smectic layer spacing is reconstructed separately through a fitted observation map based on the calculated equilibrium tilt.

papers.title: Coexistence phase of the two-dimensional Vicsek model
papers.abstract: The Vicsek model continues to be central in statistical physics studies of active matter, with major recent surprises such as the partial metastability of the famous Toner-Tu flocking phase. Here we report on the diversity of band patterns observed in its coexistence phase --some of them never observed before--, but we also argue that most disappear in the infinite-size limit, leaving nevertheless a different picture than anticipated previously. We finally show that these rather regular, globally ordered band configurations can be destroyed by a localized perturbation: the coexistence phase is also at least partially metastable, and thus must be, asymptotically, a disordered phase made of a variety of chaotically interacting traveling bands.

papers.title: Phase Diagram of the Two-Dimensional Vicsek Model
papers.abstract: Motivated by gaps in our current knowledge of the Vicsek model, we present a major update of its phase diagram in two space dimensions, summarizing comprehensive numerical simulations at length- and timescales never explored before. Our main conclusions are that multiple phase separation scenarios are at play, not just the simple microphase separation put forward in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 114, 068101 (2015)], and that the coexistence phase is subdivided in two. We also map out the region of metastability of the homogeneous Toner-Tu liquid phase.

papers.title: From particles to continuum theories in effective models of self-propelled rods
papers.abstract: Models of colliding self-propelled rods are abstractions of many real systems such as gliding bacteria and biofilaments displaced by molecular motors. They have been studied mostly in two space dimensions and shown to display a wealth of different collective regimes with many parameters involved in the ensuing phase diagrams. Continuum-level theories faithful to this phenomenology are largely lacking since coarse-graining models of explicit rods is notoriously difficult. Here we study collections of particles in which the rods geometry is taken into account effectively, by implementing the nematic alignment of their velocities and two types of repulsion. These Vicsek-style models are simple enough to be starting points for systematic coarse-graining. We thus derive hydrodynamic equations that we show to have solutions qualitatively faithful to their particle-level origin.

papers.title: Dynamic clustering of active chemotactic Janus particles
papers.abstract: Modeling self-propulsion as an emergent diffusiophoretic effect, we come back to the dynamic clustering experiment of active Janus colloids. Working in the original three-dimensional geometry, and using the chemical solute concentration as a control parameter, we find that the dynamic clustering region occupies a robust fraction of the phase diagram. This behavior is rationalized using a linear stability analysis that efficiently captures the instability of the gas phase to dynamic clusters. We also find that dynamic clustering results from the combined effects of a Keller-Segel collapse and of a motility-induced phase separation, either being arrested by the orientational coupling to the chemical field in agreement with previous work.

papers.title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers
papers.abstract: A liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) exhibits a two-way coupling between its mesogen order and network elasticity: the mesogen order sets the undeformed network conformation, and the network deformation reorients the mesogens. This coupling gives rise to large, reversible stimuli-responsive actuation, as well as to soft elasticity, a finite deformation at nearly zero stress. This article reviews the elastic theory of ideal LCEs, bridging single-chain statistics and continuum constitutive models. The "ideal" elastic behavior rests on the assumption of anisotropic Gaussian chains that retain no memory of the crosslinking state, such that rotating the director costs no free energy. The corresponding neo-classical free energy of a monodomain LCE is non-quasi-convex, with a continuous family of stress-free ground states, leading to thermally induced spontaneous deformation and soft elasticity accommodated by coexisting stripe domains. The quasi-convex relaxation of the free energy classifies the behavior of polydomain LCEs into three phases, each with a distinct macroscopic mechanical response depending on the stretch state. The ideal elastic theory can be further extended to incorporate additional behaviors and physical processes, including thermo- and photomechanical coupling, Frank elasticity from director distortion, semi-soft or non-soft behavior arising from network nonideality, and temperature- and rate-dependent viscoelasticity.

papers.title: Collective diffusion of anisotropic hard-particle mixtures
papers.abstract: Predicting the dynamics of anisotropic mixtures of different species is a challenging theoretical task. We show that Dynamical Density Functional Theory (DDFT), a theory predicting time evolution of the one-particle-density through a free energy functional, can be simplified to a diffusion equation. To quantify the dynamical relaxation behavior, we deduce corrections to the regular long-time collective diffusion coefficients from the direct correlations between the interacting particles and determine these effective diffusion coefficients analytically for a number of hard-particle systems, including mixtures of hard spheres, as well as isotropic and nematic phases of uniaxial spherocylinders and biaxial spherotriangles. Finally, we discuss how to generalize our approach to systems with positional order and suggest a possible application to predicting relaxation times of orientational order parameters.

papers.title: Capillary forces between two identical spherical particles
papers.abstract: The properties of colloidal suspensions and granular matter change drastically upon adding a small amount of liquid capable of forming capillary bridges between the solid particles. The attractive forces exerted by these liquid bridges induce the formation of particle aggregates and networks, which radically changes the macroscopic mechanical and rheological behaviour. Predicting these forces across bridge sizes, particle separations and wettability is therefore central to particle-scale modelling of capillary suspensions and wet granular matter. While the Young-Laplace equation governing the properties of the liquid bridges is well known, it lacks a convenient analytical solution. Current simulations therefore employ approximate analytic expressions, typically developed for contact angles below ~40{\deg} and bridge volumes below ~2.5% of the solid particle's volume. We compare several frequently used expressions from the literature with numerical solutions of the theoretical capillary forces. An overall good agreement is observed in the aforementioned parameter ranges, while the approximate expressions start to deviate outside their intended domains. We propose accurate and computationally efficient expressions for the capillary force that model this behaviour, for contact angles from 5{\deg} to 80{\deg} and bridge volumes from $10^{-6}$ to 0.15. We also explore mesoscopic 'fluid-scale' simulations of bridges by Multi-body Dissipative Particle Dynamics (MDPD), to ascertain whether this coarse-grained fluid model faithfully captures the continuum capillary forces. Remarkably, a good agreement is observed even for liquid bridges described by a mere few dozen fluid particles. Together, these results offer two approaches, at different resolution scales, for simulating bridges over a wide range of bridge volumes and contact angles.

papers.title: Dense granular rheology from fluctuations
papers.abstract: A governing equation for the granular temperature of flows past the jamming point is proposed and validated term-by-term with discrete element simulation. We measure and construct models for transport coefficients that do not diverge near the jamming fraction. As a limiting case of our equation, we derive the granular fluidity equation and find disagreement between the preexisting parametrizations of nonlocal granular fluidity, extended kinetic theory, and our discrete element simulations that is resolved by our continuum model.
